questions.q: A writer plots her novel on graph paper: time runs left to right, and the line rises when things go well for the heroine and falls when they go badly. Whose method is this?
choices: Freytag's pyramid, which charts rising and falling action around a central climax
Vonnegut's shapes, plotting good–ill fortune against beginning–end
McKee's value charges, marked scene by scene
Propp's functions, listed in their fixed order
questions.explain: Vonnegut's two axes are fortune (up and down) and time (left to right). Freytag charts dramatic tension, not the hero's luck.

questions.q: A trawler captain is shipwrecked, survives weeks on a raft, is rescued and ends up with a book deal and a reconciled family. Which Vonnegut shape is this?
choices: Cinderella
The Kafka shape
Man in a Hole
Boy Meets Girl
questions.explain: Someone gets into trouble, gets out of it, and ends up better off than before.

questions.q: Why does Vonnegut draw Hamlet as a flat line?
choices: Because the play has no reversal, only recognition
Because Hamlet never changes, like a sitcom character
Because tragedy, for him, is a steady fall that looks flat on his scale
Because we can't tell whether its events are good news or bad, and Shakespeare doesn't pretend to know
questions.explain: The ghost's news, and much else in the play, can't be plotted as up or down. Vonnegut admired that honesty.

questions.q: A story starts with its hero low, rises step by step to a triumph, drops at a setback (though not as low as the start), then soars to lasting happiness. Which shape?
choices: Cinderella
Icarus
Oedipus
Riches to rags
questions.explain: The staircase up, the midnight drop, and the final rise off the top of the graph are Vonnegut's Cinderella.

questions.q: A screenwriter's hero climbs out of trouble by the midpoint, seems safe, then falls again before the final climb. Which finding from the 2016 Vermont study does this echo?
choices: That rags-to-riches stories are downloaded most
That a double Man in a Hole was among the most popular arcs
That stories have exactly seven basic plots
That every story is a hero's journey
questions.explain: By Project Gutenberg downloads, Icarus, Oedipus and a fall-rise-fall-rise double hole were among the most popular arcs.

questions.q: A critic says the Vermont study can't tell a cheerful villain from a happy hero. What limit is she pointing to?
choices: It only used plays, not novels
It measured the emotional tone of the words, not what happens to the protagonist
It counted box-office takings instead of reading the books
It relied on readers' star ratings
questions.explain: Sentiment analysis scores how happy or sad the words are, so irony and contrast can mislead it.

questions.q: A young man in a dull, badly paid job wakes up as a giant insect, and things only get worse. What does Vonnegut use this shape to show?
choices: That a story can be famous and great without climbing back up
That every story needs a fall at the midpoint
That popular stories always end higher than they begin
That comedy is a living thing behaving mechanically
questions.explain: The Kafka shape starts low and goes down off the graph: no climb back, yet a classic.

ideas: A story is a line on a graph: time runs along the bottom, good and ill fortune up the side.
Somebody gets into trouble, gets out of it again, and ends up better off: people never tire of that shape.
Hamlet is a masterpiece because its line stays flat: we can never tell if its news is good or bad.
A thesis on the shapes of stories was rejected for being too simple and looking like too much fun.
